pages.title: 10th Arrondissement
pages.summary: A working district of theaters, hospitals, stations, and radical memories, close enough to fashionable Paris to serve it and resent it.

pages.title: 11th Arrondissement
pages.summary: A populous eastern district shaped by workshops, radical politics, prisons, and memories of the Commune.

pages.title: 12th Arrondissement
pages.summary: An eastern district of prisons, hospitals, rail approaches, and quieter streets where the city stores what it would rather not display.

pages.title: 13th Arrondissement
pages.summary: A southern district of hospitals, industry, and expanding neighborhoods beyond the old fashionable center.

pages.title: 14th Arrondissement
pages.summary: Montparnasse before its artistic heyday: rail yards, hospitals, prisons, quarries, and the entrances to the Catacombs.

pages.title: 16th Arrondissement
pages.summary: Passy and the western bourgeois quarters, prosperous, residential, and useful to anyone who needs wealthy clients or discreet foreign visitors.

pages.title: 17th Arrondissement
pages.summary: A district of sharp contrasts where wealthy Monceau, lively Batignolles, artists, cafés, and respectable avenues meet.

pages.title: 18th Arrondissement
pages.summary: Montmartre and Pigalle: steep streets, cabarets, studios, anarchists, dancers, drinkers, and a basilica rising over old blood.

pages.title: 1st Arrondissement
pages.summary: The ceremonial and administrative center of Paris: palaces, courts, museums, churches, and institutions layered over older violence.

pages.title: 20th Arrondissement
pages.summary: A working eastern district dominated in the visitor’s imagination by Père-Lachaise and its city of the dead.

pages.title: 3rd Arrondissement
pages.summary: A portion of the old Marais where medieval streets, archives, and the erased Temple fortress preserve stubborn traces of earlier Paris.
keyLinks: Bibliothèque Historique de la Ville de Paris

pages.title: 4th Arrondissement
pages.summary: The eastern half of the historic center, containing City Hall, old streets, and monuments built over revolutionary and Communard dead.

pages.title: 5th Arrondissement
pages.summary: The Latin Quarter’s scholarly core, crowded with students, libraries, hospitals, gardens, and institutions older than modern Paris.

pages.title: 6th Arrondissement
pages.summary: The investigators’ Left Bank territory, joining the École des Beaux-Arts, bookshops, cafés, churches, and inexpensive student life.

pages.title: 7th Arrondissement
pages.summary: The fading aristocratic Faubourg Saint-Germain, now sharing its avenues with embassies, ministries, shops, and discreet political work.

pages.title: 8th Arrondissement
pages.summary: A district of prestige, grand hotels, churches, embassies, and polished boulevards where wealth expects privacy and deference.

pages.title: 9th Arrondissement
pages.summary: A dense crossroads of theaters, opera, auctions, department stores, cafés, publishers, and occult bookshops.

pages.title: Albert de Rochas

pages.title: Alexandre Saint-Yves
pages.summary: Esoteric political thinker whose grand theories promise hidden order beneath civilization's apparent chaos.

pages.title: Alphonse Bertillon
pages.summary: Forensic pioneer whose measurement system turns bodies, criminals, and clues into sortable facts.

pages.title: Alphonse Mucha

pages.title: Anatole France
pages.summary: Elegant skeptic and author whose public disbelief may be a shield against the Yellow Sign.

pages.title: Antonio Herrera
pages.summary: Elegant Mexican seer visiting grand hotels, and perhaps not a real person at all.

pages.title: Aristide Bruant
pages.summary: Montmartre performer, impresario, and poet of the gutter with a citywide ear for rumor.

pages.title: Auguste Rodin

pages.title: Basilica of Saint-Denis

pages.title: Bicêtre Hospital

pages.title: Dépôt de Mendicité

pages.title: École des Beaux-Arts

pages.title: Folies Bergère

pages.title: Henri Matisse

pages.title: Sainte-Pélagie Prison
